newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal's Madeira sees strong 1997 tourism growth.
newsitem.headline: Portugal's Madeira sees strong 1997 tourism growth.

text.p: Portugal's mid-Atlantic holiday island of Madeira is looking forward to a sharp increase in tourism revenues this year as a stronger pound will boost spending by British visitors, a senior tourism official said.

Conceicao Almeida Estudante, Madeira's regional tourism director, told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday night that she expected total revenue from tourism in Madeira to grow by almost 20 percent this year, compared with 1996.
She said the strengthening of the pound against the escudo in recent weeks augured well for tourist visits from Britain, the second biggest source of revenue after Germany.
"British tour operators tell me that prospects for the summer are excellent, better than last year," she said.
"The stronger pound should mean the number of visiting Britons will increase and they will spend more when they get here," she said on the sidelines of a presentation about tourism in Madeira.
Almost a quarter of the half a million foreign visitors to Madeira every year are Britons, official figures show.

A senior tourism official of the sun-and-sand Algarve region of southern Portugal told Reuters earlier on Wednesday that he expected a surge in visitors from Britain this summer because of the stronger pound and the upturn of the U.K. economy.

Eliderico Viegas, head of the Association of Hotels and Tourism Businesses of the Algarve, said bookings of summer holidays by Britons were sharply higher than 1996 when the escudo was stronger and many people worried about job security.
Almeida Estudante said the strong growth in revenue from German tourists in Madeira in recent years should remain steady in 1997. Germans account for almost a third of visitors.
She said Madeira would focus its marketing efforts this year on luring young professionals in order to rely less on the affluent middle-aged who provide the bulk of its visitors.
Madeira offers a variety of open air activities to appeal to the young such as mountain biking and surfing, she said.
"A lot of young surfers have started coming to Madeira from as far away as the United States, Australia and Brazil, attracted by the challenging waves," she said.
The semi-tropical island has no beaches but offers deep sea fishing for marlin, golf, scuba diving, mountain walks and music and wine festivals.
Visitors to the smaller island neighbour of Porto Santo, which can be reached by ferry or a short flight from Madeira's capital Funchal, can relax on long stretches of sandy beach.

Almeida Estudante said she was optimistic about Madeira's medium term prospects for tourism and expected that the number of available beds would rise to 20,000 in 2000 from 17,500 now, based on an annual growth rate of some five percent.
She said Madeira was taking steps to protect its long term future, such as extending the runway at Funchal airport which would allow larger planes to fly to and from the island.
The construction work being carried out by a wholly Portuguese consortium should be completed in 1999.
